Level 2 · Intermediate · Week 12

Showcase and Celebration

Share what you built, explain how it works, and see how far you have come.

What you will learn

  • Present your project in about a minute: what it is, how one part works, and what you would add next.
  • Play everyone’s projects in a gallery walk and leave kind, specific feedback.
  • Show what you learned on the exit assessment (it is not a test you can fail: it is your stats screen).
  • Look back at your Level 2 journey, and peek at Level 3.

The big idea: look how far you have come

Twelve weeks ago you were sorting values into types. Now you have built a whole project with functions, lists, dictionaries, loops, files and tests. Here is the road you traveled:

How to explain your project

A great showcase pitch is short. Answer four questions, in this order:

  1. What is it? “This is Comet Catch. You catch comets with a rocket.”

  2. How does one part work? Pick one function, the loop, the list, the dictionary or the file. “Our next_x function gets the position and the direction and returns the new position, but never off the screen. We have a test for that.”

  3. One design decision. Why did you choose something? “The comets are circles and the rocks are squares, so you can tell them apart even without color.”

  4. What next? “Next we would add a slow mode for beginners.”

If something is not finished, that is normal. Show what works, then say what you would add next.

Exercise12.2: Gallery walk feedback

Visit every project. Play it for 2–3 minutes, then leave a card: two stars (two specific things that are good) and a wish (one kind idea). Specific is kind: “the score text is big and easy to read” helps more than “cool”.

Exercise12.4: Looking ahead to Level 3

In Level 3 you will save your code with git save points (like save points in a video game), design your own classes (blueprints for game characters and objects), and build bigger projects. The example project is Maze Muncher: a maze game where a ghost hunts you down with a clever search algorithm.

Three things I want to add to my project in a “version 2”:

SafetySharing safely

Show your project to family and friends you know. Use your nickname on the screen and in high-score files. If someone takes a photo or video, film the screen, not faces. Never upload or post your project without deciding together with a parent.

Reflect

What are you proudest of in your project?

What did you learn about working in a team?

What do you want to build next?

New words

showcase
an event where makers show their work and explain it.
pitch
a short talk that explains what your project is and why it is interesting.
design decision
a choice you made on purpose, and the reason for it.
gallery walk
visiting projects one by one, like in a museum, and leaving feedback.
version
one stage of a project; version 2 is the next, improved one.

Homework: Showcase and Celebration

15–20 minutes for the reflection. The menu is for the holidays: pick whatever you like.

CoreMy Level 2 reflection (about 10 minutes)

  1. The part of my project I am proudest of is…

  2. The hardest bug I met in Level 2 was… and I fixed it by…

  3. One piece of feedback from the gallery walk that I agree with:

  4. Something I learned about working with a partner:

  5. In Level 3 I am most curious about (git save points, classes, Maze Muncher, something else?):

ChallengeVersion 2 plan

Plan the next version of your project. Write three new features. For each one: the function you would write, what goes in, what comes out, and one test for it.

CreativeHoliday “keep coding” menu

Pick one, two, or none: holidays are for resting too. Everything works offline, with no accounts.

  • Level up: add one wish from your feedback cards to your project.

  • Art jam: make a generative art picture with a palette list, random and a function. Write down your favorite seed.

  • Secret messages: use your Caesar cipher program to send a coded note to someone at home.

  • Teach it: show a family member how to play your game, then how one function works.

  • Remix a classic: turn a past exercise (pixel art, Etch-a-sketch, word guess) into something new. Add a credit comment.

  • Unplugged: design a board game whose rules are a game loop: what happens every turn?
